question.question: An adult receives commercial liquid formula through an open feeding system in the hospital. Which practice best reduces microbial contamination?
choices: Use hand hygiene and aseptic handling, and follow manufacturer and facility preparation, storage, hang-time, and equipment-change instructions
Add fresh formula to the existing container and restart the hang-time clock with each refill
Extend the hang time whenever the formula still looks and smells unchanged
Wash and reuse equipment labeled for single use to avoid replacing the feeding system
question.rationale: Contamination prevention combines correct handling with product- and setting-specific time limits and equipment instructions. Topping off does not reset exposure time, normal appearance does not establish microbiological safety, and washing does not authorize reuse of equipment labeled for single use.

question.question: An adult receiving tube feeding develops fever and diarrhea. The feeding container has repeatedly been topped off with fresh formula instead of being replaced. Which interpretation or management plan is most defensible?
choices: Promptly assess the patient, discard the compromised formula and delivery system, and investigate contamination alongside other possible causes
Continue using the same container because each addition of fresh formula resets its safe hang time
Change to a different formula composition but keep the same container and administration set
Diagnose formula contamination from the handling error alone and defer assessment of other causes
question.rationale: Topping off is unsafe because it prolongs exposure and can introduce or propagate contamination. Stop using the compromised formula and system and replace them according to safe preparation, storage, hang-time, and equipment-change instructions. Fever and diarrhea require prompt clinical assessment; the handling error raises concern but does not establish contamination as the cause or exclude medication effects, infection from another source, or other intolerance.

wholeBodyReview.heading: Monitor delivery and metabolic safety
wholeBodyReview.body: Compare the prescribed regimen with the formula and water actually delivered, including interruptions and their causes. Track weight trend, intake and output, hydration and volume status, gastrointestinal symptoms, glucose, sodium, potassium, magnesium, phosphate, and kidney function. Set the monitoring interval according to acuity, the stage of feeding, and clinical changes rather than applying one schedule to every patient. For patients at refeeding risk, check and treat potassium, magnesium, and phosphate abnormalities during cautious initiation; severely low levels warrant delaying initiation or calorie increases until corrected. Rapid falls or levels that are difficult to correct require prompt reassessment, electrolyte treatment, and adjustment of energy delivery. Inspect tube position, patency, and the access site; report new pain, excess leakage, redness, or swelling. Reduce contamination risk with hand hygiene, aseptic handling, and manufacturer and facility instructions for preparation, storage, hang time, and equipment changes. Do not top off a feeding container or reuse equipment labeled for single use. Fever or diarrhea warrants clinical assessment of contamination and other possible causes rather than a diagnosis based on a handling error alone.
